name: Executive Order of February 25, 1874 enlarging the Skokomish Reservation on Hood Canal
citation: Executive Order of February 25, 1874, reprinted in Executive Orders Relating to Indian Reserves (1902), p. 134
nations: S'Klallam bands party to the 1855 Treaty of Point No Point
promises: This was an addition, not a cession: the President enlarged the Skokomish reservation on Hood Canal, first set apart by the Treaty of Point No Point of January 26, 1855, with a tract running from the mouth of the Skokomish River upstream and north to Hood Canal (Royce).
The Interior Department treats the 1855 treaty and this 1874 order as the two documents that established the Skokomish Reservation (Solicitor's Opinion M-37034, 2016).
today: In 2016 the Interior Solicitor reaffirmed a 1971 opinion that the whole width of the Skokomish River along the reservation border is part of the reservation, with the riverbed held in trust for the Tribe. The opinion notes that in Skokomish Indian Tribe v. France (9th Cir. 1963) the court held tidelands along the reservation passed to Washington State at statehood; that ruling went against the Tribe.

nationVoice.summary: The Tribe says that around 1900 a Tacoma tycoon took the land between the channels at the mouth of the Skokomish River and diked it, destroying plants such as basketry sweetgrass, that Washington State's claim to the tidelands cut its shellfish gathering, and that these losses became land claims.

sources.title: Royce, Indian Land Cessions in the United States (18th Annual Report of the Bureau of American Ethnology, 1899), schedule entry 559 (Executive Order of February 25, 1874)
Solicitor's Opinion M-37034, Boundary of the Skokomish Reservation along the Skokomish River, January 15, 2016
sources.publisher: U.S. Department of the Interior, Office of the Solicitor

openQuestions: The order gave land to the Skokomish, so no promise of its own was found to have been broken. The 1855 Treaty of Point No Point, its ICC claim (Docket 296, compromise settlement of 1963) and the Cushman dam litigation belong to the treaty's own file and were not reviewed here.
Washington's Department of Fish and Wildlife has disputed the 2016 riverbed opinion, per press reports; the dispute was not researched further.

treaties.json names the tribe 'Sklallam (Skokomish)' and lists the Jamestown, Lower Elwha and Port Gamble S'Klallam tribes; Royce names the reserve Skokomish, and whether S'Klallam people shared in this addition was not checked.
The Skokomish Indian Tribe's own website was not reached; no account by the Tribe of the 1874 order was recorded.
